entry: Fibrous [[Connective tissue|connective tissue]] joining one [[Bone|bone]] to another and forming [[Joint|joints]]. Ligaments are made mostly of collagen fibers. They are similar to [[Tendon|tendons]], which connect [[Muscle|muscle]] to bone, and to fasciae, which connect muscles to other muscles. Ligaments cannot usually be regenerated naturally. They are viscoelastic: they stretch under tension and return to shape, but overstretching weakens the joint and makes it prone to dislocation. Some ligaments limit a joint's range of motion. Joint instability can over time wear the cartilage and eventually lead to [[Osteoarthritis|osteoarthritis]]. The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL), crucial to knee stability, is one of the most often torn. Artificial ligaments made of synthetic [[Polypropylene|polypropylene]] and other polymers are sometimes used in reconstructive surgery. About 900 ligaments are found in an average adult human body.

Electronic component giving off light from a [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] when [[Electric current|current]] passes through it. Electrons in the semiconductor recombine with electron holes, releasing energy as [[Photon|photons]]. The color of the light depends on the energy needed for electrons to cross the band gap of the semiconductor. White light is produced by combining several semiconductors or by coating the device with a light-emitting phosphor. The first practical LEDs, introduced in 1962, emitted low-intensity [[Infrared|infrared]] light, and the first visible ones were dim and red. Early LEDs served as indicator lamps and in seven-segment displays. Later types emit visible, [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] and infrared light. LEDs use less power than incandescent bulbs, produce less waste heat, last longer and switch faster. In the early 1990s Shuji Nakamura, Hiroshi Amano and Isamu Akasaki developed blue LEDs, which brought white lighting and full-color displays into practical use. They won the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Unit of length equal to the distance light travels in a vacuum in one Julian year. Used in [[Astronomy|astronomy]], especially for distances to [[Star|stars]] in popular science, it equals exactly 9460730472580.8 km, about 9.46 trillion kilometers or 5.88 trillion miles. Despite its name, it measures distance, not time. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) defines it using the Julian year of 365.25 days and the [[Speed of light|speed of light]]. Professional astronomers more often use the [[Parsec|parsec]], about 3.26 light-years. The unit appeared a few years after Friedrich Bessel measured the distance to the star 61 Cygni in 1838, finding it to be 660,000 [[Astronomical unit|astronomical units]]. The IAU abbreviation is ly.

Tower or other structure fitted with lamps and lenses to serve as a navigational beacon. Lighthouses mark dangerous coastlines, [[Shoal|shoals]], reefs and rocks, and safe entries to [[Harbor|harbors]]; some also aid aerial navigation. The most famous lighthouse of antiquity, the Pharos of [[Alexandria]], Egypt, collapsed after a series of earthquakes between 956 and 1323. Modern lighthouses developed from about the turn of the 18th century, as trade grew and their function shifted from marking ports to warning of hazards. Henry Winstanley built the first lighthouse fully exposed to the open sea, on the Eddystone Rocks in the [[English Channel]], from 1696 to 1698. John Smeaton's rebuilding of 1756 to 1759 set the prototype for later designs, using a form of [[Concrete|concrete]] that sets underwater. The Fresnel lens, invented in the 1820s by [[Augustin-Jean Fresnel]], uses prisms to concentrate light into stronger beams. The number of operational lighthouses has since declined because of maintenance costs and cheaper electronic navigation.

Deliberate use of artificial or natural light to achieve practical or aesthetic effects. Daylighting, which uses windows, skylights or light shelves, can supply light during the day and save energy, since artificial lighting is a major component of energy use in buildings. Proper lighting enhances task performance, improves the appearance of an area and can have positive psychological effects. Early lighting came from fire, followed by oil lamps of stone, shell and horn, filled with grease. Whale oil was a major fuel until Abraham Gesner, a Canadian geologist, refined [[Kerosene|kerosene]] in the 1840s. Gas lighting powered street lights in major cities from the early 1800s, and [[Electric light|electric lighting]] spread from the 1880s. Fixtures hold the light source, direct light and limit glare; their efficiency is usually measured in [[Lumen (unit)|lumens]] per [[Watt|watt]]. Modern [[Light-emitting diode|light-emitting diodes]] are efficient and long-lived.

Top professional [[Association football|association football]] league in France. Contested by 18 clubs, it runs from August to May and operates promotion and relegation with Ligue 2. The league was inaugurated in 1932 under the name National and adopted its current name in 2002. Top finishers qualify for European competitions such as the [[UEFA Champions League]]. Paris Saint-Germain is the most successful club, with 14 league titles.

Song by American singer-songwriter [[Bob Dylan]], a 1965 single. Dylan wrote its lyrics in June 1965, after returning exhausted from a tour of England, and distilled a long draft into four verses and a chorus. He recorded it a few weeks later as the opening track of *Highway 61 Revisited*, with an improvised Hammond organ riff by Al Kooper. [[Columbia Records]] hesitated to release the six-minute song, but after a leaked copy reached influential DJs it was issued as a single on July 20, 1965. It reached No. 2 on the U.S. Billboard charts and became a worldwide hit. The song completed Dylan's transformation from folk singer to rock star and is considered one of the most influential compositions in postwar popular music. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked it No. 1 on its "500 Greatest Songs of All Time" lists in 2004 and 2010. [[Jimi Hendrix]] covered it. In 2014 Dylan's handwritten lyrics sold at auction for $2 million, a record for a popular music manuscript.

Major right-wing political party in Israel. Founded in 1973 by Menachem Begin and [[Ariel Sharon]] as an alliance of right-wing parties, its name means "The Consolidation." Its 1977 election victory marked the first time the left had lost power and the first time a right-wing party won the most votes. [[Benjamin Netanyahu]] has led the party since 2005, apart from a brief interruption, and served as prime minister in 1996–1999, 2009–2021 and from 2022. The party won the most seats in the 2026 [[Israel|Israeli]] legislative election, with 27.

American rapper and record producer, regarded as a progenitor of the club-oriented [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] subgenre crunk. Born in Atlanta, Georgia, he is the frontman of the group Lil Jon & the East Side Boyz. His production and voice were instrumental in crunk's commercial breakthrough in the early 2000s. He produced hits including Ying Yang Twins' "Salt Shaker" and Ciara's "Goodies," and his work on [[Usher (musician)|Usher]]'s "Yeah!" won him a Grammy Award for Best Rap/Sung Performance. His 2013 single "Turn Down for What," with DJ Snake, is an [[Electronic dance music|EDM]] track certified 8× platinum by the Recording Industry Association of America. Its video passed one billion views on [[YouTube]] in 2020.

American rapper, singer and record executive. Born and raised in [[New Orleans]], he was signed to Cash Money Records at age 11 and was its flagship artist until 2018. He is often regarded as one of the most influential [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] artists of his generation. *Tha Carter III* (2008) sold over one million units domestically in its first week and won the Best Rap Album [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]]. In 2012 he became the first male artist to surpass [[Elvis Presley]] for the most entries on the Billboard Hot 100. He founded Young Money Entertainment in 2005; it signed [[Drake (musician)|Drake]] and [[Nicki Minaj]].

Lily family of [[Monocotyledon|monocotyledonous]] flowering plants in the order Liliales. The family includes about 15 genera and 610 species, mostly herbaceous perennials that grow from bulbs or rhizomes. Its flowers typically have six petal-like tepals, six stamens and a superior ovary. First described in 1789, the family was long a catch-all group of lilioid monocots, including genera now placed in other families. Its members are widely distributed, mainly in temperate regions of the [[Northern Hemisphere]], and their flowers are usually insect-pollinated. Many, including [[Lilium|lilies]] and [[Tulip|tulips]], are important ornamental plants. Some species are poisonous to humans and household pets, and some have been eaten as famine food. The family likely evolved between 82 and 52 million years ago.

Female figure in late-antique Mesopotamian and Jewish mythology. Lilith does not appear in the [[Hebrew Bible]], but the Hebrew word *lilit* appears in [[Isaiah]] 34:14, where its meaning is debated and the King James Version renders it "screech-owl." She is named in the [[Dead Sea Scrolls]] and in later Mandaean and Jewish sources. The [[Talmud|Babylonian Talmud]] mentions her, and medieval Jewish folklore said she fled the [[Garden of Eden]] rather than submit to Adam. The Alphabet of Sirach (c. 700–1000 AD) presents her as Adam's first wife, created from the same clay. Jewish incantation bowls and amulets identify her as a female [[Demon|demon]]. Some rabbinic authorities, including [[Maimonides]], rejected her existence.

Genus of bulbous, herbaceous flowering plants, the true lilies. About 119 species are recognized in the genus, most native to the temperate and subtropical [[Northern Hemisphere]]. The flowers are large and often fragrant, in colors including white, yellow, orange, pink, red and purple, with six tepals that may spread or curl back. The plants grow from scaly bulbs without a tunic. The Latin name derives from the Greek *leírion*, generally taken to refer to white lilies. True lilies are highly toxic to [[Cat|cats]]. Lilium is one of the world's leading ornamental genera, with thousands of [[Cultivar|cultivars]] and [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]] grown in gardens and for cut flowers.

City (pop., 2023: 238,246), capital of the Hauts-de-France region in northern France. Lille lies on the Deûle River near the [[Belgium|Belgian]] border and is the center of the European Metropolis of Lille, with 1,195,234 inhabitants (2023). Lille passed to France under [[Louis XIV]] after the War of the Spanish Succession. A manufacturing center from the 16th century, it became a major textile and machinery city during the [[Industrial Revolution]], but its industries declined from the 1960s. Conversion to services in the 1990s and the arrival of the TGV and [[Eurostar]] in 1994 transformed the city. Lille was a European Capital of Culture in 2004 and was named World Design Capital for 2020.

American actress of the [[Silent film|silent]] era. Gish acted on stage as a child and entered film in 1912, becoming a leading figure through her work with director [[D. W. Griffith]]. She starred in Griffith's *The Birth of a Nation* (1915), the highest-grossing film of the silent era, and in *Intolerance* (1916), *Broken Blossoms* (1919) and *Way Down East* (1920). *Vanity Fair* dubbed her the "First Lady of the Screen" in 1927. She moved into sound films with *Duel in the Sun* (1946), for which she received an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actress, and *The Night of the Hunter* (1955). She retired after *The Whales of August* (1987), opposite [[Bette Davis]] and [[Vincent Price]]. She received an honorary Academy Award in 1971 and a Kennedy Center Honor in 1982, and in later years she promoted the preservation of silent film.

City (pop., 2020: 1,122,000), capital and largest city of [[Malawi]]. Lilongwe lies in the central region near the borders with [[Mozambique]] and [[Zambia]] and is an important economic and transportation hub for central Malawi. It is named after the Lilongwe River. The population was 989,318 at the 2018 census, up from 674,448 in 2008. Founded as a *boma* around 1902, it became an administrative center in 1904 and was recognized as a town in 1947. Malawi's first president, Hastings Kamuzu Banda, chose it in 1965 as a growth point, and it became the capital in 1975, replacing Zomba. The last government offices moved there in 2005.

American actress and comedian. Tomlin began in [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up comedy]] and became known on the variety show *Rowan & Martin's Laugh-In* (1969–1973). Her one-woman Broadway show *The Search for Signs of Intelligent Life in the Universe*, written by Jane Wagner, won a Tony Award for Best Actress in a Play. Her film debut was *Nashville* (1975), for which she received an Academy Award nomination. She starred with [[Jane Fonda]] in *9 to 5* (1980) and in the [[Netflix]] series *Grace and Frankie* (2015–2022). Tomlin has won seven Emmy Awards and a Grammy Award and received the Kennedy Center Honor in 2014.

Eurasian woodland plant (*Convallaria majalis*) with sweetly scented, bell-shaped white flowers. Growing 15–35 cm (6–14 in) tall, it spreads by underground rhizomes to form colonies and is native to [[Eurasia]]. Its six white tepals, fused into a bell with reflexed tips, open in late spring and are followed by poisonous orange-red berries. The plant is highly poisonous because of cardiac glycosides, and it has been used in [[Traditional medicine|traditional medicine]] for heart conditions. Its flowers are used in floristry, and perfumes have been based on its scent, though no aromatic extract can be made from the plant itself. The genus name, coined by [[Carl Linnaeus]], comes from the Vulgate translation of the Song of Songs. The species was once placed in the [[Liliaceae|lily family]].

City (pop., 2023: 10,092,000), capital and largest city of [[Peru]]. Lima lies in the desert of the central coast, overlooking the [[Pacific Ocean]], and is the country's political, cultural, financial and commercial center. Its metropolitan area forms a contiguous urban area with the seaside city of Callao, where the seaport and airport are located. Around one-third of Peru's population lives in the metropolitan area. The city was founded in 1535 as the City of Kings and became the capital of the Viceroyalty of Peru, and later of the republic after independence. Lima hosted the 2019 Pan American Games, the largest sporting event ever held in the country, and will host them again in 2027. It also hosted [[Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation]] meetings in 2008, 2016 and 2024.

[[Legume|Legume]] (*Phaseolus lunatus*) grown for its edible seeds. Also called butter bean, sieva bean, double bean or Madagascar bean, it has two gene pools. The large-seeded lima type was domesticated in the Andes around 2000 BC, and the small-seeded sieva type in [[Mesoamerica]] around AD 800. The [[Moche culture]] of Peru cultivated lima beans heavily. Exports from the Spanish viceroyalty were labeled "Lima, Peru," which gave the beans their name. In the United States it is a warm-season crop, grown in Delaware and the mid-Atlantic for processing and in the Midwest and California for dry beans. The seeds contain cyanogenic glycosides that release [[Cyanide|hydrogen cyanide]] if eaten raw or undercooked, so they must be boiled or processed before eating.

Small, round to oval [[Citrus|citrus]] fruit with green flesh and a sour taste. Limes are the fruit of several Citrus species, most of them hybrids; the key lime and Persian lime are the most economically important. Limes are usually harvested green, when their flavor and acidity are strongest. Lime juice and zest flavor drinks and dishes such as [[Cocktail|cocktails]], [[Ceviche|ceviche]] and key lime pie. Limes are a rich source of [[Vitamin C|vitamin C]]. They originated in tropical Southeast Asia and spread through human migration and trade. In the 19th century British sailors ate citrus, including limes, to prevent [[Scurvy|scurvy]], which gave rise to the nickname "limey." In 2023 world production of limes, combined with lemons, was 23.6 million tonnes, led by [[India]] and [[Mexico]].

Carbonate [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rock]], the main source of lime. It is composed mostly of the minerals [[Calcite|calcite]] and aragonite, which are forms of [[Calcium carbonate|calcium carbonate]] (CaCO₃). Limestone forms when these minerals precipitate from water containing dissolved calcium, mainly through biological processes such as the accumulation of [[Coral|corals]] and shells in the sea. It often contains fossils that reveal ancient environments. Most limestone formed in shallow marine environments. Because it is slightly soluble in rainwater, exposed limestone erodes into [[Karst|karst]] landscapes, and most [[Cave|cave]] systems are found in limestone bedrock. Limestone formations contain about 30% of the world's petroleum reservoirs. It is used to make [[Cement|cement]] for [[Concrete|concrete]], as road aggregate, and as a white pigment or filler in paint and toothpaste.

Value that a function's output approaches as its input nears a given point. The limit of a function f at p is L if f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x sufficiently close to p, though the function need not be defined at p. The limit does not exist if inputs very close to p give outputs that stay a fixed distance apart. Limits underpin [[Continuous function|continuity]], which holds when a function's limits agree with its values, and the [[Derivative|derivative]], the limiting slope of secant lines to a graph. The modern epsilon-delta definition was introduced by [[Karl Weierstrass]] in 1861, building on work by Bernard Bolzano in 1817. [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]] discussed limits in *Cours d'analyse* (1821). The arrow below the limit symbol is due to [[G. H. Hardy]], who introduced it in *A Course of Pure Mathematics* (1908).

Value that the terms of an infinite [[Sequence|sequence]] tend toward, if one exists. A sequence is convergent if it has a finite limit and divergent otherwise. A number L is the limit if the terms become arbitrarily close to L and stay that close after some point. For example, the sequence 1/n converges to 0. The limit of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n grows is the number [[E (mathematical constant)|e]]. Limits can be defined in any [[Metric space|metric space]] or [[Topological space|topological space]], but are usually first encountered in the real numbers. Bernard Bolzano gave a modern definition in 1816 and Karl Weierstrass in the 1870s. The concept is described as the fundamental notion on which [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]] rests.

Science of inland aquatic [[Ecosystem|ecosystems]], including [[Lake|lakes]], reservoirs, rivers and [[Wetland|wetlands]]. Limnology studies the biological, chemical, physical and geological characteristics of fresh and saline inland waters, including ponds, streams, springs, groundwater and inland salt lakes. It examines the [[Drainage basin|drainage basin]], the movement of water through it and the biogeochemical changes that occur along the way. The name comes from the Greek *límnē*, meaning lake. François-Alphonse Forel coined the term, establishing the field through his studies of Lake Geneva and describing it as "the oceanography of lakes." In 1922 August Thienemann and Einar Naumann co-founded the International Society of Limnology. Landscape limnology considers ecosystems together with their drainage basins, and global limnology studies the role of inland waters in Earth's biogeochemical cycles.
